section.title: Cylindrical coordinates in integrals
section.p: ended with a warning. Rectangular coordinates are not always the natural language of a solid. A box likes x, y, and z. A can, a pipe, a cone, and a round tank ask for radius, angle, and height.

Cylindrical coordinates keep the height z, but replace x and y by polar coordinates: x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta,\qquad z=z. Here r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} is the distance from the z-axis, and \theta is the angle around that axis.

The new coordinates make circular solids easier to describe. They also change the small volume piece. A tiny box in r,\theta,z is not a rectangular box in ordinary space. That is why the factor r appears.

subsection.title: The volume element r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz
subsection.p: Start with the simplest round solid: a cylinder of radius 3 and height 5: x^2+y^2\le 9,\qquad 0\le z\le5. In cylindrical coordinates this becomes 0\le r\le3,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad 0\le z\le5.

At radius r, an angular change \Delta\theta gives an arc length approximately r\,\Delta\theta. So the small piece has volume approximately \Delta V \approx (\Delta r)(r\,\Delta\theta)(\Delta z) = r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta\,\Delta z. Thus the cylindrical volume element is \boxed{dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz.}

exercise.title: Where does the r come from?

statement.p: A small cylindrical piece spans \Delta r, \Delta\theta, and \Delta z. Two such pieces share the same three numbers, but one sits near the z-axis and the other sits far from it. Why are their volumes different, and why does that difference force the factor r into dV=r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta?

hint.p: Think about the arc swept out by a fixed angle \Delta\theta. How long is that arc at radius r? The wider arc far from the axis is exactly what the factor r records.

figure.caption: The angular side of a small polar rectangle has length approximately r\,\Delta\theta, not \Delta\theta.

statement.p: Let U be a bounded closed parameter region with piecewise smooth boundary, using r\ge0 and an angular interval of length at most 2\pi. Suppose T(r,\theta,z)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z) covers E=T(U) once except for boundary seams and the axis. For a continuous function f on a neighborhood of E, \iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV =\iiint_U f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)\,r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz. Use bounds describing U in the chosen order of iterated integration. The axis and seam do not affect the integral. Repeated coverage of the interior would count volume more than once.

subsection.p: We supply this general rule for use. The tiny-box picture explains its factor; the next exercise proves it for every continuous integrand on a specified cylinder, using planar polar integration. The exercise does not prove the rule for every region.

exercise.title: Derive the rule on a cylinder by slicing

statement.p: Let E=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2\le1,\ 0\le z\le1\}, and let f be continuous on a neighborhood of E. Cartesian slicing gives \iiint_E f\,dV=\iint_{x^2+y^2\le1}G(x,y)\,dA,\qquad G(x,y)=\int_0^1 f(x,y,z)\,dz. You may use this fact: integrating a continuous function over a fixed closed interval gives a continuous function of the remaining variables on this closed base. Apply planar polar integration to G, then substitute its definition to obtain the cylindrical formula for f on this cylinder. Which step supplies the factor r?

solution.p: The supplied continuity fact allows the planar polar rule: \iint_{x^2+y^2\le1}G\,dA =\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1G(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta =\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_0^1 f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta. The factor comes from the planar polar theorem. This argument works for every such f, rather than checking only the volume case f=1.

subsection.p:
Now compute the cylinder's volume:
V \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3\int_0^5 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3 5r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{45}{2}\,d\theta \amp= 45\pi.
This agrees with the familiar formula \pi r^2h=\pi(3)^2(5)=45\pi.

The factor r is not optional. If we forgot it, we would get \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3\int_0^5 1\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=30\pi, which is not the volume of the cylinder. The error comes from pretending that angular pieces near the axis and angular pieces far from the axis have the same width. They do not.

aside.title: Optional: oriented-volume connection
aside.p: A covector is a linear scalar measurement on vectors. If \alpha,\beta,\gamma are three covectors on the same vector space, define their triple wedge by its value on an ordered triple (u,v,w): (\alpha\wedge\beta\wedge\gamma)(u,v,w)= \det\begin{pmatrix} \alpha(u)&\alpha(v)&\alpha(w)\\ \beta(u)&\beta(v)&\beta(w)\\ \gamma(u)&\gamma(v)&\gamma(w) \end{pmatrix}. Linearity in each row makes this expression linear in each covector. Swapping two covectors changes its sign, and repeated covectors give zero. We also use (\alpha\wedge\beta)\wedge\gamma for this triple determinant. This convention suffices here; it is not a construction of wedge multiplication in all degrees.

For variable coefficients, evaluate all covectors at the same fixed parameter point. Here dx means the differential of the scalar function x(r,\theta,z) on the parameter domain, and similarly for dy; dz is its height-coordinate measurement. Thus all three act on the same parameter vectors. We have dx=\cos\theta\,dr-r\sin\theta\,d\theta,\qquad dy=\sin\theta\,dr+r\cos\theta\,d\theta. Multilinearity, alternation and the two-covector rule give dx\wedge dy=r\,dr\wedge d\theta,\qquad dx\wedge dy\wedge dz=r\,dr\wedge d\theta\wedge dz. The wedge expression records orientation in order (r,\theta,z); ordinary volume uses the absolute determinant. Iterated integration order alone does not specify orientation. develops explicit pullback notation for this substitution.

exercise.title: Optional: three measurements and signed volume

statement.p: Using the determinant definition in , justify linearity in each covector, sign reversal on swapping two covectors, and vanishing when two agree. Then use the displayed expressions for dx,dy,dz to verify the cylindrical triple-wedge identity. This extension is independent of the ordinary integration exercises.

solution.p: These are respectively multilinearity in a determinant row, change of sign on interchanging rows, and vanishing for equal rows. Expansion gives coefficients r\cos^2\theta and r\sin^2\theta in front of dr\wedge d\theta\wedge dz; the two repeated-factor terms vanish. Their sum is r. This proves the local triple identity under the stated convention, without asserting a general associativity theorem.

subsection.title: Cylinders, cones, and rotational symmetry
subsection.p: Cylindrical coordinates are especially good when equations contain x^2+y^2. The translation is x^2+y^2=r^2.
For example, the circular cylinder x^2+y^2=9 becomes r=3. The solid inside the cylinder becomes 0\le r\le3.
The calculation was short because the solid did not care about the angle \theta. Every vertical slice through the z-axis looked the same.

exercise.title: Why do round shapes feel at home here?

statement.p: Cylinders, cones, and paraboloids all become tidy equations like r=3, z=4-r, or z=r^2 in cylindrical coordinates, while a plain box turns awkward. What do these round solids have in common that makes a coordinate built from r, \theta, and z describe them so cleanly?

hint.p: Ask what happens to each solid if you spin it around the z-axis. Which variable does its boundary equation quietly ignore?

subsection.p: When the solid and the integrand do not depend on \theta, we can usually factor out the full turn: \int_0^{2\pi} d\theta=2\pi. For a rotationally symmetric solid, E=\{(r,\theta,z):0\le\theta\le2\pi,\ a\le r\le b,\ g_1(r)\le z\le g_2(r)\}, and an integrand depending only on r and z, we get \boxed{\iiint_E f\,dV = 2\pi\int_a^b\int_{g_1(r)}^{g_2(r)} f(r,z)\,r\,dz\,dr.} The factor 2\pi comes from going once around the axis. The factor r comes from the widening of angular pieces.

statement.p: A metal pipe has inner radius 1, outer radius 2, and length 5. Its density is \delta(r)=4+r kilograms per cubic meter. The density is larger near the outer wall.

subsection.title: Choosing bounds in cylindrical coordinates
subsection.p: For cylindrical coordinates, the shadow is usually drawn in the xy-plane using polar coordinates. Then z runs from a lower surface to an upper surface, as in .
A useful routine is:

li.p: Rewrite the equations using x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta,\qquad x^2+y^2=r^2.
Describe the shadow in the xy-plane by bounds on r and \theta.
Describe the vertical bounds for z.

subsection.p: For a solid of the form \alpha\le\theta\le\beta, \qquad a(\theta)\le r\le b(\theta), \qquad g_1(r,\theta)\le z\le g_2(r,\theta), the integral becomes \boxed{\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV = \int_\alpha^\beta \int_{a(\theta)}^{b(\theta)} \int_{g_1(r,\theta)}^{g_2(r,\theta)} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta.}

figure.caption: The slanted-roof solid and its disk shadow 0\le r\le2 in the xy-plane. At the marked point (r,\theta), the red vertical segment runs from z=0 to z=3+r\cos\theta. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

image.shortdescription: 3D slanted-roof cylinder above a disk shadow, with a radial arrow and a vertical integration segment.

example.title: A cylinder cut by a slanted roof

statement.p: Let E be the solid inside the cylinder x^2+y^2\le4, above the floor z=0, and below the plane z=3+x. In cylindrical coordinates, x=r\cos\theta. So the top surface is z=3+r\cos\theta. Since 0\le r\le2, this top height is at least 1, so it stays above the floor.

The shadow is the disk 0\le r\le2,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. Therefore \boxed{V = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_0^{3+r\cos\theta} r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta.} Compute:
V \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2 (3+r\cos\theta)r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi} \left[ \frac32 r^2+\frac13r^3\cos\theta \right]_0^2 d\theta \amp= \int_0^{2\pi} \left( 6+\frac83\cos\theta \right)d\theta \amp= 12\pi.
The slanted part averages out around the full circle: \int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\,d\theta=0.

subsection.p: The bounds can also count too much if we are careless. For the full cylinder, the bounds 0\le\theta\le4\pi go around the same solid twice. The integral then gives twice the volume. Coordinate seams are harmless when they only repeat a boundary, such as \theta=0 and \theta=2\pi. They are not harmless when they repeat a whole three-dimensional region.

subsection.title: Applications to solids of revolution and tubes
subsection.p: A solid of revolution is often easiest to describe by drawing its rz-profile. The angle \theta then spins that profile around the z-axis.

example.title: A vase from a rotating profile

statement.p: A small vase has height 3. At height z, its radius is R(z)=1+\frac z3. So it widens linearly from radius 1 at the bottom to radius 2 at the top.

subsection.p: This example also explains why the old disk method from single-variable calculus worked. At height z, the cross-section is a disk of radius R(z), so its area is \pi R(z)^2. Cylindrical coordinates produce the same expression: \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{R(z)} r\,dr\,d\theta = \pi R(z)^2. The factor r is exactly what makes the circular area come out correctly.

A tube is similar, except the radial interval does not start at 0. If the inner radius is a and the outer radius is b, then a\le r\le b. A washer cross-section comes from the same idea: \int_0^{2\pi}\int_a^b r\,dr\,d\theta = \pi(b^2-a^2).

statement.p: A solid of revolution is made by spinning a flat profile around the z-axis. If you slice the result into thin cylindrical tubes, each tube has a radius r and a tiny thickness. Why does this picture of nested tubes match a solid of revolution so naturally, and where in the volume integral does the factor r for each tube appear?

hint.p: Imagine the surface of one thin tube at radius r. As you go once around in \theta, how far does that surface travel? That circumference is what the r in r\,dr\,d\theta is keeping track of.

subsection.p: Cylindrical coordinates solve every problem whose geometry is organized around an axis. But they still treat height z differently from the other two coordinates. A ball does not have a preferred height direction. Its natural coordinate is distance from the center. Once we use that distance, two angles are needed to say which way we are looking. The price is another scale factor: \rho^2\sin\phi.
